questions.q: What is the specific chemical modification that alkaline phosphatase performs on a DNA molecule?
questions.a: Alkaline phosphatase hydrolyzes the 5'-phosphate group from the terminal nucleotide of DNA, leaving a 5'-hydroxyl group. A wrong answer (e.g., "removes 3'-phosphate" or "adds phosphate") reveals confusion about the directionality of DNA ends and the substrate specificity of the enzyme — a critical error because ligation requires a 5'-phosphate, so removing it prevents ligation, while removing a 3'-phosphate would not.

questions.q: A student treats a linearized plasmid vector with alkaline phosphatase, then adds a PCR-amplified insert (with no 5'-phosphates) and DNA ligase. The ligation fails. Explain why.
questions.a: DNA ligase requires a 5'-phosphate on one strand and a 3'-hydroxyl on the other to form a phosphodiester bond. Alkaline phosphatase removed the 5'-phosphates from the vector, and the PCR product lacks 5'-phosphates (unless phosphorylated primers were used). Thus, neither fragment has a 5'-phosphate, so ligation cannot occur. A wrong answer (e.g., "alkaline phosphatase destroys the vector") shows misunderstanding of the enzyme's reversible role and the absolute requirement for 5'-phosphate in ligation.

questions.q: You have a vector digested with BamHI (sticky ends) and an insert digested with BglII (compatible sticky ends). You want to prevent vector self-ligation but allow directional cloning. Which enzyme treatment(s) would you apply and in what order?
questions.a: Step 1: Treat vector with alkaline phosphatase to remove 5'-phosphates (prevents self-ligation). Step 2: Treat insert with T4 polynucleotide kinase (if it lacks 5'-phosphates) to add them. Step 3: Ligate. Since BamHI and BglII produce compatible ends but different overhang sequences (GATC vs GATC), the ligation is not inherently directional; however, phosphatase treatment ensures only vector-insert ligation occurs. A wrong order (kinase before phosphatase) or omitting kinase for non-phosphorylated insert reveals failure to track phosphate status on each fragment.

questions.q: Compare and contrast the action of S1 nuclease and Klenow fragment on a DNA fragment with a 5' overhang. Which enzyme would you use to create a blunt end, and why?
questions.a: S1 nuclease degrades single-stranded DNA, so it will chew back the 5' overhang to create a blunt end (but may also degrade the complementary strand). Klenow fragment (3'→5' exo⁻) fills in 5' overhangs using its polymerase activity, creating a blunt end without degrading the opposite strand. For precise blunt-end creation, Klenow is preferred. A student who chooses S1 nuclease for a 5' overhang shows confusion: S1 is for removing single-stranded tails (e.g., after hairpin opening), not for filling in.

questions.q: Evaluate the statement: "Alkaline phosphatase treatment is always necessary when cloning into a plasmid vector cut with a single restriction enzyme." Justify your answer with a counterexample.
questions.a: The statement is false. If the vector is cut with two different restriction enzymes (directional cloning) producing non-compatible ends, self-ligation is impossible because the ends don't match. Alkaline phosphatase is then unnecessary. Also, if using a vector with a lethal gene or positive selection (e.g., ccdB), self-ligation is selected against. A student who says "always necessary" fails to recognize that phosphatase is only needed when vector ends are compatible and can self-ligate.

questions.q: Design a cloning strategy to insert a blunt-ended PCR product (no 5'-phosphates) into a plasmid vector linearized with EcoRV (blunt ends). Specify every enzyme treatment, order, and reason.
questions.a: 1. Treat vector with alkaline phosphatase (prevents self-ligation of blunt ends). 2. Treat PCR product with T4 polynucleotide kinase (adds 5'-phosphates required for ligation). 3. Ligate with T4 DNA ligase. 4. Transform. Alternative: Use a PCR product amplified with phosphorylated primers (skip kinase). A poor answer omits kinase, uses phosphatase on insert, or suggests cohesive-end enzymes for blunt ends — showing inability to integrate enzyme functions into a complete workflow.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Alkaline phosphatase is the answer: it snips off the ______'-phosphate groups from the vector ends, so DNA ligase cannot form the phosphodiester bond.
What common mix-up does this lesson flag about Alkaline phosphatase?
questions.a: Students often believe alkaline phosphatase "destroys" DNA ends or that it acts on 3' ends.

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: Student can explain the specific role of alkaline phosphatase in preventing vector self-ligation, distinguish its action from T4 polynucleotide kinase, and design a cloning strategy that selects the appropriate DNA-modifying enzyme for a given restriction digest scenario (blunt vs sticky ends, directional vs non-directional cloning).
